en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
The Chapter on Turning Back, 33. The Training Rule on Causing Discomfort.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Thullanandā was learned, an eloquent speaker, confident, and capable of delivering a discourse on the Dhamma.
Bhaddā Kāpilānī also was learned, an eloquent speaker, confident, and capable of delivering a discourse on the Dhamma, being highly esteemed and held in high regard by people.
People—
“Venerable Bhaddā Kāpilānī is learned, an eloquent speaker, confident, capable of delivering a discourse on the Dhamma, and highly esteemed.
Having first paid homage to Bhaddā Kāpilānī, they afterwards paid homage to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
The bhikkhunī Thullanandā was overcome by jealousy.
Thinking, “These people, it seems, are of few desires, contented, secluded, and unattached,
yet they dwell with much persuasion and much entreaty,” he would walk back and forth, stand, sit, and lie down in front of Bhaddā Kāpilānī;
he would recite to her, have her recite to him, and perform his own study as well.
Those bhikkhunīs who were few in desires … [as before] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can the noble lady Thullanandā intentionally cause discomfort for the noble lady Bhaddā Kāpilānī? … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, bhikkhus, that the bhikkhunī Thullanandā intentionally causes discomfort for Bhaddā Kāpilānī?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked her:

“… How can the bhikkhunī Thullanandā intentionally cause discomfort for Bhaddā Kāpilānī? This is not suitable, bhikkhunīs. … [as before] … “Bhikkhunīs, how indeed could the bhikkhunī Thullanandā intentionally cause discomfort for Bhaddā Kāpilānī?”
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, the nuns should recite this training rule:
‘If any nun should intentionally cause discomfort to another nun, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).’”
"But whichever" means whichever such...
"nun" means... [as before].
...pe... this is the meaning of "bhikkhunī" intended in this context.
"Of a bhikkhunī" means of another bhikkhunī.
"Intentionally" means:
knowing, perceiving, and having willed and intended, there is a transgression.
"Causes discomfort" means:

If, thinking, “By this, she will be made uncomfortable,” one walks, stands, sits, lies down, recites, causes another to recite, or performs a private recitation in front of her without having asked permission, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one who is fully ordained perceives another as fully ordained and intentionally makes her uncomfortable, there is an offense of expiation.
If one who is fully ordained is uncertain [of the other’s status] and intentionally makes her uncomfortable, there is an offense of expiation.
If one intentionally causes discomfort for someone who is fully ordained, perceiving them as not fully ordained, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
If one intentionally causes discomfort for someone who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one causes discomfort for someone who is not fully ordained, perceiving them as fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she is unsure whether the person is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she perceives one who is not fully ordained as not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense—

If, not wishing to cause discomfort, she walks, stands, sits, or lies down in front [of a monk] after having asked for permission; or if she recites, causes [him] to recite, or performs a private recitation [in his presence],
she is free from offense— provided she is insane or a first-time offender.
The third training rule is concluded.
